title: The Studio Opens
tagline: You see where this year leads, and you measure where you are starting from.
objectives: I know what this year builds: I make real work, I learn to judge it, and I get better at choosing.
I know the studio code, which is the DT room rules, and I can judge whether somebody is keeping it.
I can find my way around this website, and I know what my Portfolio Zero and my Compass are for.

config.headline: The Studio is open.
lines: Your Digital Technology year has a name, and the name is the Studio. It is not a real room in this school. It is what we call your DT year, because this year you work the way a studio works: you make things, you look hard at them, and you decide what to do next. You have seventeen Studio lessons this year, one every fortnight.

This is your last year of Digital Technology before GCSE, and it builds three things you can point at afterwards. You CREATE real work: programs you write yourself, data you turn into something worth reading, web pages you design for somebody else to use. You learn to JUDGE work, your own and other people's, against a standard instead of a feeling. And you get better at CHOOSING, because you will have real evidence about what you are good at. Those three are worth having whatever subjects you end up taking.

There is one particular thing that evidence is useful for. In JANUARY you pick your GCSE options. Digital Technology is one of the subjects on that list and it is optional: plenty of people will pick it, plenty will not, and both of those are fine answers. If you do pick it, there are two routes inside it, Multimedia and Programming, and by January you will know far more about which kind of work suits you. If you do not pick it, everything this year teaches you is still yours.

One thing about the screens you clicked through to get here. Those were Google's own permission screens, and they were asking whether this website is allowed to know who you are, so that your work saves under your name. You only see them the very first time you sign in. You will not see them again.

Here is what this hour holds, in order. First a short look around this website, which takes about seven minutes. Then the studio code: six real situations, and you decide whether each one is in line with the code or against it. Then Portfolio Zero, which is twelve quick questions about where you are starting from, and it is not a test. Then your Compass, which asks what kind of work you actually enjoy. It finishes with a card about where the year goes next, one marked question, and a screen that asks you how the hour went.
config.help: This card types itself out. Read it through — your teacher may be reading it with the class — and press the button at the bottom when you are ready to move on. Nothing here is marked.

config.intro: There are five things to find on this screen. This website is where every Studio lesson lives, so seven minutes now saves you asking all year. Each step tells you what to look for and what you will SEE when you have found it.

steps.title: You already know where your year map is
steps.text: Your year map is the page you came from to get here, and it holds all seventeen lessons in six groups, with a heading over each group. Look at the top left of this screen: the button there says Year map, and it takes you back at any time. Do not press it now — you come back to your year map at the end of the lesson.
steps.confirm: I can see the Year map button at the top left

steps.title: A locked tile is normal, not a fault
steps.text: Most of the tiles on your year map have a small padlock on them. Nothing is broken. Your teacher opens each lesson on the day you do it, so a locked tile just means the class has not got there yet. Only the lesson you are working on is open.
steps.confirm: I understand what a locked tile means

steps.title: Watch your work save itself
steps.text: Look along the top of this screen, over on the right, for a small green word: Saved. You never press a save button here. Every time you answer something or finish a part of a lesson, this website writes it to your own record, and that green word tells you it has landed. Your work follows your login, so you can pick it up on any school computer.
steps.confirm: I found the Saved chip at the top

steps.title: Find the help button
steps.text: Look at the bottom right of this screen for a round button with a question mark on it. Click it now. A panel opens with help for the part of the lesson you are on right now, so it says something different on every screen. Close it again when you have read it.
steps.confirm: I opened the help button and read what it said

steps.title: Open your Wardrobe
steps.text: Click your name in the top right corner. Your Wardrobe opens. Every real studio has a wardrobe department, the people who look after how everything looks: this one is yours, and it holds the looks your screen can wear. You earn them by finishing lessons, and anything you unlock stays yours for the rest of the year, even if your points move around later. You have not earned anything yet, so most of what you can see is still padlocked. Close it and come back here.
steps.confirm: I opened my Wardrobe and saw what is in it

config.help: Work down the steps one at a time. Each one says exactly what to look for and what you should see when you have found it. Tick the box under a step once you have done it, and the next step appears. If you cannot find something, ask the pupil beside you where they clicked.

config.intro:
These are the DT room rules. They are the same six rules every DT room in this school runs on, and there is nothing new in them — what is new is the job you are given here.

A working studio writes its rules down as a code of conduct, and then somebody has to decide whether people are keeping it. Today that somebody is you. You will read six real situations. For each one you decide whether it is IN LINE with the code or AGAINST it, and if it is against it, which standard it breaks.

Watch out for one thing: not every case is somebody doing something wrong. Nothing wrong here is a real answer, and it is the right answer more than once.

stretch.title: Two cases where the rules disagree with each other
stretch.text:
That is the studio code done, and you have judged all six cases.

There are two more and they are optional. They are harder in a particular way: in each one, two of the rules pull in opposite directions, and you have to decide which one comes first. There is a right answer to both, and it is worth thinking about.

Have a go if you want one, or press Stop here instead and move on with the lesson. Nothing is taken off you either way.

items.stem: A pupil finishes early. She leaves her machine with her work still on the screen, goes out at the bell, and does not come back.
options: Against the code — she left her machine signed in
Against the code — she left her area untidy
Against the code — she moved somebody else's equipment
Nothing wrong here

items.stem: A pupil notices that the mouse at her station has stopped working. She tells the teacher before she starts, and carries on at a different machine.
options: Nothing wrong here
Against the code — she should have fixed it herself
Against the code — she moved to a different machine
Against the code — she should have waited until the end of the lesson to say

items.stem: A pupil brings a bottle of water in from break and stands it on the desk beside the keyboard while she works. The lid is on.
options: Against the code — no drinks near the machines, lid or no lid
Against the code — she should have asked first
Nothing wrong here, because the lid is on
Nothing wrong here, because water does no harm

items.stem: The class arrives at the room before the teacher does. The pupils wait outside in a line until she comes and opens the door.
options: Nothing wrong here
Against the code — they should have gone in and got started
Against the code — they should have gone to find the teacher
Against the code — waiting outside wastes lesson time

items.stem: A pupil's headphones will not reach, so she unplugs the cable from the back of the machine beside hers and plugs it into her own.
options: Against the code — nothing gets unplugged or moved
Against the code — she should have used the machine beside hers instead
Nothing wrong here, because she put it back afterwards
Nothing wrong here, because it was only a cable

items.stem: At the end of the lesson a pupil signs out, but leaves her chair pulled out and a sheet of notes on the desk because the bell has gone.
options: Against the code — she left her area untidy
Against the code — she did not sign out
Nothing wrong here, because she signed out
Nothing wrong here, because the bell had gone

items.stem: SENIOR CASE. A pupil's machine freezes halfway through the lesson. Her work is still on the screen, she is still signed in, and nothing she clicks does anything. The teacher is at the far side of the room. What should she do?
options: Go and tell the teacher now, and say the machine is frozen with her still signed in
Try the cables at the back until it starts working again
Move quietly to a free machine and say nothing, so the lesson is not held up
Wait at the frozen machine until the teacher happens to come over

items.stem: SENIOR CASE. A pupil sits down and finds the machine already signed in as somebody from the last class, with that pupil's work open on the screen. What should she do?
options: Sign that person out without reading anything, then tell the teacher
Close the work and carry on as that person, so nothing is lost
Read enough of it to work out whose it is, then go and find her
Leave it exactly as it is and use it, because she did not sign it in

config.help: Read each case, then click the answer that matches it. Each one is marked the moment you click, and you are told why. Nothing wrong here is a real answer and it is right more than once, so do not go looking for a fault in every case.

config.sealBody: Twelve answers, kept as the record of where you were on day one. You read it back before your options in January, and again in the last lesson of the year.
config.intro:
This part is called Portfolio Zero. A portfolio is the collection of work somebody shows to prove what they can do, and this is yours before you have made any of it — the zero at the start.

There are twelve quick questions. Nine of them are about things you might be able to work out, and three of them just ask how you feel about your own work. It is NOT a test and you cannot fail it. Most of the nine are about things you have not been taught yet, so not knowing is completely normal.

This one is only about what you can DO. Later in the hour there is a second activity called your Compass, and that one asks something different: what you ENJOY.

You will not be told right or wrong on any of them, and that is on purpose. You read this back twice: once before your options in January, and once in the last lesson of the year, when you will see for yourself how far you have come.
config.solo: You do this one on your own, quietly — nobody is told right or wrong here, so there is nothing to compare.

items.stem: A program is given these three instructions, in this order: set the total to 10, add 5 to the total, then print the total. What appears on the screen?
options: Nothing, because it was never told to add up

items.stem: A list holds four songs. The second song is taken out of the list. How many songs are in the list now, and where has the fourth one moved to?
options: Three songs, and the last one has moved up a place
Three songs, and nothing else has moved
Four songs, with a gap where the second was
Three songs, and they are now in a different order altogether

items.stem: A program is supposed to add up a shopping list, and every total it gives is exactly double what it should be. What would you check FIRST?
options: Whether each price is being added twice
Whether the computer is broken
Whether the screen is showing the wrong number
Whether the list has too many items in it

items.stem: A club counts its members every year: 40, 44, 48, 52. Somebody says 'our club is growing fast'. What do those four numbers actually show?
options: It grows by the same small amount each year
It doubles every year
It grows faster every year
It is not growing at all

items.stem: You want a computer to tell photographs of cats apart from photographs of dogs. What does it need before it can do that?
options: Lots of example photographs, already labelled cat or dog
One photograph of a cat and one of a dog
A written description of a cat
Nothing — computers already know what animals look like

items.stem: A website answers a question you typed and sounds completely certain. What should you do before you use the answer in your work?
options: Check it against somewhere else that is worth trusting
Use it, because it sounded certain
Change a few words so it is in your own writing
Ask a friend whether it sounds right

items.stem: Two apps do the same job. In one, the button you need is on the first screen. In the other, it is three menus deep. Which is the better design, and why?
options: The first, because the thing people do most should be easiest to reach
The second, because it looks tidier
The first, because fewer screens means less work for the computer
Neither — how it looks is what matters

items.stem: You have designed a poster page with pale grey writing on a white background. Who is most likely to struggle with it, and what would help?
options: Anyone who does not see low contrast well — darker writing would help
Nobody, as long as the words are spelled correctly
Only people using a small screen — a bigger screen would help
Only people in a hurry — shorter words would help

items.stem: You have finished a program and it works when you try it. How do you know it is actually finished?
options: You try it on the awkward cases too, not just the one you had in mind
It worked once, so it is finished
It is finished when the deadline arrives
You ask somebody else whether they like it

items.stem: NO RIGHT ANSWER — be honest. How do you feel about making something look professional, so that somebody else would take it seriously?
options: I would not know where to start
I can do a bit of it
I am reasonably confident
It is one of the things I am best at

items.stem: NO RIGHT ANSWER — be honest. How do you feel about making code do what you want it to do?
options: I would not know where to start
I can do a bit of it
I am reasonably confident
It is one of the things I am best at

items.stem: NO RIGHT ANSWER — be honest. How do you feel about working out whether something you read online is actually true?
options: I would not know where to start
I can do a bit of it
I am reasonably confident
It is one of the things I am best at

config.help: Twelve quick questions, and nothing here is marked. You will not be told right or wrong, on purpose: this is a record of where you are starting from, and it is only useful if it is honest. The last three ask how you FEEL about your own work — there is no right answer to those at all, so say what is true. If you do not know one of the others, pick what seems most likely and keep going.

config.intro:
Portfolio Zero asked what you can DO. Your Compass asks something completely different: what you actually ENJOY.

There are three questions and each one gives you two things to choose between. Neither side is better than the other, and there is no right answer. Pick the one that sounds more like you, even if it is only slightly more.

At the end a needle settles and you are told, in plain words, what it found. If you pick all three on one side it lands firmly there. If you split them, it settles near the middle — which is a real answer too, and the most common one.
config.note: Your Compass decides nothing. It is where you are standing today, and today is the first day of the year. You look at it again before your options in January, and people do change their minds.
config.boardTitle: Which one sounds more like you?
config.boardLead: Pick one from each pair. You can change any of them until you press the button at the bottom.
config.lockedNote: Pick one from all three pairs, and the button below wakes up.

pairs.q: A group project needs a poster and it needs the code behind the website. You get first pick.
pairs.design: I would rather design the poster
pairs.build: I would rather write the code

pairs.q: Something you made is not working properly and nobody knows why.
pairs.design: I would rather work out how to explain the problem to everyone else
pairs.build: I would rather sit with it and keep trying things until it works

pairs.q: You have a free afternoon and a computer.
pairs.design: I would rather tell a story with it — a video, a page, a piece of music
pairs.build: I would rather solve a puzzle with it — a game, a program, a bit of data

design.title: You lean to the designing and communicating side
design.say:
That means the part of this work you enjoy most is making something OTHER PEOPLE will look at, read, watch or use. Designing it, laying it out, choosing how it feels, getting the message across. It is a real skill and there is a lot of it in this year.

That is the useful answer, and it is true whatever you go on to study.
design.route: And if you do pick GCSE Digital Technology in January, that side of the work is the Multimedia route.

mixedDesign.title: You are close to the middle, leaning slightly to designing and communicating
mixedDesign.say:
You picked two answers on one side and one on the other, so you have not landed firmly on either. That is not you failing to decide. It is the honest answer for most people on the first day of a year, and plenty of people stay there.

What it does tell you is which way you tipped: slightly towards making things OTHER PEOPLE look at, read, watch or use.
mixedDesign.route: GCSE Digital Technology has both sides in it, Multimedia and Programming, and you have until January to see which one pulls harder. You are also allowed to decide the subject is not for you.

mixedBuild.title: You are close to the middle, leaning slightly to building and problem-solving
mixedBuild.say:
You picked two answers on one side and one on the other, so you have not landed firmly on either. That is not you failing to decide. It is the honest answer for most people on the first day of a year, and plenty of people stay there.

What it does tell you is which way you tipped: slightly towards making things WORK, and finding out why they do not.
mixedBuild.route: GCSE Digital Technology has both sides in it, Multimedia and Programming, and you have until January to see which one pulls harder. You are also allowed to decide the subject is not for you.

build.title: You lean to the building and problem-solving side
build.say:
That means the part of this work you enjoy most is making something WORK. Writing the instructions, finding out why it is not doing what you meant, getting it right in the end. It is a real skill and there is a lot of it in this year.

That is the useful answer, and it is true whatever you go on to study.
build.route: And if you do pick GCSE Digital Technology in January, that side of the work is the Programming route.

config.resultNote: Nothing has been decided here. Your Compass is saved so you can look at it again before your options in January, and you can answer these three questions differently then.
config.help: Three either/or questions about what you ENJOY, not what you are good at. There is no right answer and nothing is marked. Pick one from each pair, then press the button to settle the needle. Nothing you pick here decides anything — you look at it again in January.

config.intro: One card to look at before you go, so you know where the year is heading.

steps.title: Two routes, one shared start
steps.text: This picture is the map of GCSE Digital Technology. Everyone who takes it does the same core work first, and then it splits into two routes: Multimedia, which is the designing and communicating side, and Programming, which is the building and problem-solving side. You do not choose between them today. Digital Technology is one of the subjects on your options list in JANUARY, and it is optional. Deciding it is not for you is a perfectly good decision, and this year is worth doing either way. Your next lesson is called First Words in Python, and you write real code in it. Nothing is assumed: it starts from your very first line.
steps.imgAlt: A flat diagram. One wide block on the left is labelled The shared core, everybody does this. An arrow leads from it to two blocks side by side on the right: Multimedia, designing and communicating, and Programming, building and problem-solving. Underneath, a line reads: you choose in January, and you can choose neither.
steps.imgCap: The two GCSE Digital Technology routes, and the core work everybody does first.
steps.confirm: I know where this year is heading

config.help: One card about where the year goes, with a picture of the two GCSE routes. Read it and press the button to move on. Nothing here is marked and nothing here is a decision.

config.intro: One last question, and this one IS marked. Your teacher sees how the class did on it, so answer it on your own.

items.stem: Which of these is TRUE about the two GCSE Digital Technology routes, going by what this lesson has told you?
options: They share the same core work, and you would choose between them in January if you pick the subject at all
Your Compass has already chosen one of them for you
They are completely separate subjects from the very first day
Everybody in this class has to pick one of the two

config.help: One question about the year itself, and this one IS marked. You are told whether you were right, and why, at the very end of the lesson — after the How did it go? screen.

config.alreadyFiled: This lesson report went to your teacher the first time — looking back through it never overwrites it.
